config.title: Design Permission System

intro.title: Design Permission System
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a simple permission system that controls what users can see and do in a React application. You'll learn how to use TypeScript interfaces to define user roles and permissions in a structured way. The main technologies involved are React components, TypeScript interfaces, and conditional rendering based on user permissions. By the end, you'll have a basic system that shows or hides UI elements depending on whether a user has admin, editor, or viewer access.
intro.usecase: Permission systems are fundamental to enterprise applications where different user roles need access to specific features. In admin dashboards, permissions control which users can view analytics, manage user accounts, or configure system settings. Content management systems use permissions to determine who can publish articles, edit drafts, or moderate comments. E-commerce platforms restrict access to inventory management, order processing, and financial reports based on user roles. These systems ensure data security and appropriate functionality distribution across teams and departments.

objectives: Define TypeScript interfaces to model user roles and permissions with specific properties
Implement permission checking functions that return boolean values based on user roles
Apply conditional rendering in React components to control UI visibility based on permissions
Use React hooks to manage and access permission state within functional components
Construct higher-order components to wrap and protect route components with permission logic
Execute permission validation before allowing access to protected application features
Store permission configurations in a centralized object for consistent access across components
Retrieve user permissions from context or props to make authorization decisions
Modify component behavior dynamically by passing different permission sets as props
Compare user roles against required permissions to determine access eligibility
Handle permission changes by updating state and triggering component re-renders
Control application routing by implementing permission-based route guards

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package. This will allow you to create React components and manage state in your permission system.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported, making React and useState available for use in your component.
successCriteria: The code should include a valid import statement that imports both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you the foundation to build React components with state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react' using the correct import syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the PermissionSystem component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named PermissionSystem that returns JSX. Use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Start by defining a component that returns a simple JSX element like a div.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the PermissionSystem component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The PermissionSystem component is defined and returns JSX.
successCriteria: The code includes a component named PermissionSystem that returns JSX (e.g., a div).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the PermissionSystem component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named PermissionSystem that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component definition is missing or incorrect. Ensure you create a functional component named PermissionSystem that returns JSX.

steps.title: Define the Permission type interface
steps.instruction: Inside the PermissionSystem component, define a TypeScript interface named 'Permission' with three properties: 'id' (string), 'name' (string), and 'enabled' (boolean).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a Permission interface that defines the structure for permission objects with typed properties.
successCriteria: The code should contain an interface named Permission with id: string, name: string, and enabled: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the Permission interface with the correct TypeScript types. This interface will help ensure type safety when working with permission data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has all three required properties (id, name, enabled) with the correct TypeScript types (string, string, boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The Permission interface isn't defined correctly. Make sure to use the 'interface' keyword, name it 'Permission', and include all three properties with their types.

steps.title: Initialize permissions state with sample data
steps.instruction: Inside your PermissionSystem component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'permissions'. Initialize it with an array containing at least two sample Permission objects. Make sure to provide the TypeScript type annotation for the state.
steps.hint: Remember to use the Permission interface you defined earlier. Your state should look like: const [permissions, setPermissions] = useState<Permission[]>([...]) with sample objects inside the array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a state variable 'permissions' initialized with sample data, properly typed as an array of Permission objects.
successCriteria: The code should include: 1) useState hook call, 2) state variable named 'permissions', 3) TypeScript type annotation Permission[], 4) array with at least two sample Permission objects matching the interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the permissions state with properly typed sample data. This gives us a starting point to work with in our permission system.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use useState? Is the state variable named 'permissions'? Did you provide the Permission[] type annotation? Does the array contain at least two sample Permission objects with id, name, and allowed properties?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the PermissionSystem component, use useState to create a state variable called 'permissions' with the type Permission[] (array of Permission objects). Initialize it with at least two sample objects that match the Permission interface you defined earlier.

steps.title: Create togglePermission handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your PermissionSystem component, create a function named togglePermission that takes a permission id (number) as a parameter and toggles the allowed status of that permission in the state.
steps.hint: You'll need to use the setPermissions state setter function to update the state. Create a new array where you find the permission with the matching id and toggle its allowed property.
steps.expectedOutcome: A togglePermission function is defined inside the component that properly updates the permissions state when called with a permission id.
successCriteria: The togglePermission function should be defined with a typed parameter (id: number), use setPermissions to update state, and correctly toggle the allowed property of the matching permission.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the togglePermission handler function with proper TypeScript typing. This function will allow us to toggle individual permissions in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are a few issues. Make sure your togglePermission function: 1) Takes an id parameter typed as number, 2) Uses setPermissions to update state, and 3) Correctly toggles the allowed property for the matching permission.
steps.feedbackWrong: The togglePermission function is missing or incorrect. You need to create a function that takes a permission id and toggles its allowed status in the state array.

steps.title: Add main container div to component return
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a <div> element with the className 'permission-system' as the main container for your permission system. This div should wrap around the existing <h1> element.
steps.hint: Place a <div> with className='permission-system' around your existing content. Remember to close the div tag properly.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component's return statement should now have a <div> with className 'permission-system' that wraps the <h1> element, creating a proper container structure.
successCriteria: The existing <h1> is wrapped inside this div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added the main container div with the correct className. This provides a proper structure for your permission system UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a <div> with className='permission-system' that wraps around the <h1> element. Check your syntax and nesting.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main container div is missing or incorrect. You need to add a <div> with className='permission-system' that wraps the existing <h1> element.

steps.title: Add a heading to display the component title
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add an h1 element with the text 'Permission System'.
steps.hint: The h1 element should be placed directly inside the opening and closing div tags.

successCriteria: The h1 element is inside the container div
The h1 contains the exact text 'Permission System'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the component title heading.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added an h1 element with the exact text 'Permission System' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The heading wasn't added correctly. Check that you've placed an h1 element with 'Permission System' text inside the container div.

steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, after the heading, use the map method on the permissions state array to create a <div> element for each permission. Each div should have a key attribute set to permission.id.
steps.hint:

steps.expectedOutcome: The component will render a <div> for each permission in the state, each with a unique key.
successCriteria: The code includes a map call on the permissions array, returns a <div> element for each item, and sets the key attribute to permission.id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully mapped through the permissions array to create a list of div elements. Each div has a unique key, which is essential for React's rendering performance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but something is missing. Make sure you're using the map method on the permissions array, returning a <div> for each permission, and setting the key attribute to permission.id.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to use the map method on the permissions state array to create a <div> element for each permission. Each div must have a key attribute set to permission.id.

steps.title: Display permission name in each item
steps.instruction: Inside the map callback, add a <span> element to display each permission's name property.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to output the permission name from the current permission object.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each permission item now shows its name (e.g., 'Read', 'Write', 'Delete') inside a span element.
successCriteria: The code must include a <span> element inside the map callback that displays permission.name using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed each permission's name in the UI. This shows how to access and render state data within JSX.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a <span> element and displaying permission.name with curly braces inside the map callback.
steps.feedbackWrong: The permission names aren't being displayed. Check that you added a <span> with {permission.name} inside the map callback.

steps.title: Add toggle button to each permission item
steps.instruction: Inside each permission item, add a button element with text 'Toggle' and wire its onClick event to call togglePermission with the current permission's id.
steps.hint: Place the button inside the same div as the permission name. Use onClick={() => togglePermission(permission.id)}.

steps.expectedOutcome: Each permission item now displays a 'Toggle' button that, when clicked, will call togglePermission with the correct id.
successCriteria: The button element must be inside the mapping div, have text 'Toggle', and its onClick must call togglePermission(permission.id).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added interactive toggle buttons to each permission item.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check if it's inside the mapping div, has text 'Toggle', and the onClick correctly calls togglePermission with permission.id.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly configured. Make sure to add a button element with onClick handler inside each permission item.

steps.title: Display enabled status on toggle button
steps.instruction: Inside the button element, use a ternary operator to conditionally set the button text to 'Enable' when permission.allowed is false, and 'Disable' when permission.allowed is true.
steps.hint: You can use permission.allowed ? 'Disable' : 'Enable' as the button text content.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each toggle button will now display 'Enable' when the permission is not allowed, and 'Disable' when the permission is allowed.
successCriteria: The button text should dynamically change between 'Enable' and 'Disable' based on the permission.allowed value using a ternary operator.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented conditional rendering for the button text based on the permission's allowed status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary operator with permission.allowed to conditionally display 'Enable' or 'Disable'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button text isn't conditionally rendering based on permission.allowed. Try using permission.allowed ? 'Disable' : 'Enable' inside the button element.

steps.title: Add visual indicator for permission status
steps.instruction: Add a className to each permission item's div that changes based on the permission's allowed status. Use a ternary operator to set the class to 'permission-item allowed' when allowed is true, and 'permission-item denied' when false.
steps.hint: Add className attribute to the div that wraps each permission item. Use a template literal or ternary operator to conditionally set the class string.

steps.expectedOutcome: Each permission item div will have a className that visually indicates its status (allowed or denied) through CSS classes.
successCriteria: Add className attribute to permission item div

steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added conditional CSS classes to visually indicate permission status. The UI now provides clear visual feedback about which permissions are allowed or denied.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Added the className attribute to the div, 2) Used permission.allowed in a ternary operator, 3) Included both 'permission-item' base class and conditional 'allowed'/'denied' classes.
